title: Final Project
text:
Research Questions
For my final project I wanted to explore anomaly detection methods, so I chose a credit card fraud detection dataset. The questions I sought to answer were:

How well do unsupervised ensemble-based models detect fraudulent transactions when labels are withheld during training?
How do distance-based and statistical approaches to outlier detection compare to ensemble-based methods in identifying rare but meaningful anomalies?

title: Final Project
text:
Data
This project uses the Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset, containing transactions made by European cardholders over two days in 2013. The dataset includes 284,807 transactions, with only 492 labeled as fraudulent, making it highly imbalanced. It is important to note that the features V1 through V28 are only numerical input variables, done via PCA transformation. This is due to privacy concerns, per the acknowledgements section on the Kaggle page. The only features that are not transformed are “Time” and “Amount.” The “Class” feature is the response variable where a value of 1 refers to a fraudulent transaction and 0 is a valid transaction.

title: Final Project
text:
Models & Scoring
I use three unsupervised approaches that look at outlierness from different angles. In all cases, larger scores mean the transaction is more suspicious. Labels are withheld during fitting and used only for evaluation.

title: Final Project
text:
Evaluation
I evaluated the models in three ways:

ROC-AUC. Measures overall ranking quality across all thresholds. This is the probability that a randomly chosen fraudulent transaction receives a higher score than a randomly chosen valid transaction. Higher is better.
PR-AUC. Focuses on the positive class and is more informative with severe class imbalance. It summarizes the precision–recall trade-off and is the primary metric here given the ~0.17% fraudulent transaction rate.
Top-N precision (precision at N). Sort scores from highest to lowest and look at the first N alerts. I set N to the number of frauds in the test set.

Larger values are better for all three metrics. I emphasize PR-AUC and precision at N for imbalanced data, and I include ROC-AUC to show overall ranking strength. Labels are withheld during fitting and used only to compute these metrics.


kNN-distance: ROC AUC=0.9552 | PR AUC=0.1112
Bagged-kNN: ROC AUC=0.9549 | PR AUC=0.1182
GMM: ROC AUC=0.9330 | PR AUC=0.1374

title: Final Project
text:
Results

How well do unsupervised ensemble-based models detect fraudulent transactions when labels are withheld during training? On the held-out test split (85,443 rows; fraud rate 0.173%), the models trained without labels separate fraudulent transactions from valid transactions in a meaningful way. The GMM model attains the highest PR-AUC score (0.137) and the highest precision at N (0.223) when I set N = int(y_test.sum()) the result is 148, which equals the number of fraudulent transactions in the test set. The kNN distance model, scored as the average distance to the 20 nearest neighbors, achieves the top ROC-AUC (0.955).
How do distance-based and statistical approaches to outlier detection compare to ensemble-based methods in identifying rare but meaningful anomalies? Relative to the distance-based model, Bagged-kNN (25 bags, 70% subsamples; scores averaged) shows a modest and consistent performance improvement on PR-AUC (0.118 vs 0.111) and on precision at 148 (0.189 vs 0.169), which is consistent with variance reduction helping in a rare-event setting. Comparing families, the statistical/density approach (GMM) outperforms both distance-based methods on PR-AUC (0.137) and precision at 148 (0.223), while the distance-based approach (kNN distance) retains the best ROC-AUC (0.955).

title: Detecting Anomalies in Credit Card Transactions
text:
Data

Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset (European cardholders, 2013, two days).
284,807 transactions; 492 labeled fraud (≈0.172%).
Features: V1–V28 (anonymized via PCA), Time and Amount.
Labels (Class) withheld during training; used only for evaluation.

title: Detecting Anomalies in Credit Card Transactions
text:
Models & Scoring

Ensemble-based: Bagged-kNN — 25 bags, 70% subsamples, each bag computes kNN distance (k = 20); scores are averaged to reduce variance.
Distance-based: kNN distance (k = 20) — anomaly score is the distance to the k-th neighbor.
Statistical: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) — n_components = 3, covariance = full; anomaly score is negative log-density via -score_samples
